Abstract—Predicting early allograft failure (EAF) after 
living donor liver transplantation remains challenging due to 
its low incidence. We developed a hybrid framework that 
incorporates Isolation Forest –derived anomaly scores as 
auxiliary features into an XGBoost classifier to address severe 
class imbalance in a cohort of 4,973 patients (EAF prevalence: 
2.55%). The hybrid model achieved an AUROC of 0.80 
outperforming the baseline XGBoost model and suggesting that 
anomaly-based feature augmentation can enhance the detection 
of rare adverse events in transplant outcome prediction. 
Clinical Relevance —Anomaly-based feature augmentation 
may improve early allograft failure prediction in liver 
transplantation. 
I. INTRODUCTION 
Early allograft failure (EAF) following living donor liver 
transplantation (LDLT) is a rare clinical outcome, and, like 
other rare conditions, the resulting severe class imbalance 
poses a fundamental barrier to the accurate identification of 
high-risk minority patient groups by machine learning 
models [1, 2]. While gradient boosting algorithms such as 
XGBoost have established themselves as the state -of-the-art 
for tabular data analysis, they are prone to bias toward the 
majority class in environments dominated by normal cases. 
Consequently, there is a significant risk that these models 
will overlook subtle precursor p atterns in the minority 
positive class, dismissing them as noise. To address this, we 
propose a hybrid machine learning framework that integrates 
outlier metrics derived from unsupervised learning as key 
features within a supervised model. 
II. METHODS 
This retrospective study analyzed 4,973 adult LDLT 
recipients at Asan Medical Center (Seoul, South Korea) with 
an EAF prevalence of 2.55% (IRB No. S2025-1475-0002). 
A total of 26 preoperative variables were included, including 
donor and recipient demographics, comorbidities, 
perioperative clinical characteristics, and transplantation - 
related features. The dataset was partitioned into training 
(75%, n = 3,730) and independent test (25% , n = 1,243) sets 
using stratified random sampling. Within the training set, 
25% was allocated for validation, and Bayesian optimization 
based on repeated stratified 3 -fold cross -validation was 
performed to optimize the model.

Y. Han and H. Shin are with the Department of Medical Science, 
Graduate School, University of Ulsan; the Department of Digital Medicine, 
Asan Medical Center; and the Brain Korea 21 Project, University of Ulsan 
College of Medicine, Seoul 05505, South Korea. H. Shin is also with the 
Institute of Digital Healthcare, University of Ulsan College of Medicine , 
Seoul, South Korea (e-mail: hangsik.shin@amc.seoul.kr). 
To specifically enhance the detection of rare classes, we 
applied Isolation Forest [3], a tree -based unsupervised 
learning algorithm. This method relies on the principle that 
outliers are susceptible to isolation with fewer splits than 
normal data. The Isolation Forest was fitted exclusively on 
the training set. Consequently, identifying instances with 
shorter path lengths as likely abnormal, we calculated an 
anomaly score and integrated it as a feature into the XGBoost 
model. We compared the performance of this hybrid 
approach against a baseline XGBoost model trained solely on 
the 26 preoperative variables. 
III. RESULTS 
For the independent test set, the hybrid model (XGBoost 
+ Isolation Forest) showed improved performance over the 
baseline XGBoost (Table 1): area under the receiver 
operating characteristic curve (AUROC) rose from 0.75 to 
0.80, area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) from 
0.11 to 0.14, positive predictive value (PPV) from 0.08 to 
0.12, and F1-score from 0.14 to 0.19. 
IV. DISCUSSION & CONCLUSION 
This study demonstrates that integrating unsupervised 
anomaly detection into a supervised learning framework 
effectively mitigates the inherent class imbalance in medical 
datasets. Specifically, by suppressing false positives and 
enhancing prediction precision through the utilization of 
anomaly scores, this hybrid approach offers a more robust 
predictive framework than conventional methods for 
forecasting critical rare adverse events such as EAF. These 
findings highlight the high potential of this approach for 
implementation in clinical decision support systems, where 
the early identification of high-risk rare cases is essential.
